New England Puritans
noo ING-luhnd PYOOR-i-tuhnz
noun
From New England + Puritan; the English Calvinist settlers of seventeenth-century Massachusetts and Connecticut.

Biblical Definition

The New England Puritans were the English Calvinist settlers who, fleeing the corruptions and persecutions of the Old World, planted in Massachusetts, Connecticut, and the neighboring colonies a society ordered, in their intention, by the Word of God. They held a covenantal theology, a congregational church order, the regulative principle of worship, and a vision of a community in covenant with God—a city upon a hill, as Winthrop preached, whose obedience or disobedience would be visible to all. They prized preaching, catechism, the Sabbath, learning (founding Harvard for a literate ministry), and the searching of the heart for the marks of saving grace. Their literature of practical divinity—the diaries, the sermons, the casuistry—remains among the richest in the English tongue. Yet their record is mingled: the genuine piety stood alongside grave failures, including the injustice done to the native peoples and the tragedy at Salem, where the fear of witchcraft overran the bounds of biblical justice. The dictionary honors the Puritan recovery of experiential, covenantal, Word-governed religion, while measuring the failures of the colonies by the same Scripture they professed, that the children of light might learn from both their fidelity and their sin.

Webster 1828 Definition

The English Calvinist settlers of seventeenth-century New England; covenantal, congregational, Word-governed in intention, with rich piety and mingled failures.

NEW ENGLAND PURITANS, English Calvinist settlers of seventeenth-century New England.

Held covenant theology, congregational order, and the regulative principle of worship.

Prized preaching, catechism, the Sabbath, and learning; founded Harvard for the ministry.

Left a rich literature of practical divinity and self-examination.

Mingled record: genuine piety alongside injustice to natives and the Salem tragedy.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:14 — "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."

Deu 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

2Co 13:5 — "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?"

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Modern Corruption

The Puritans are caricatured as joyless tyrants or idealized as flawless saints; both miss the mingled record of genuine piety and real sin.

expand to see more

The modern caricature of the Puritan—a joyless, repressive bigot—is a corruption born of ignorance and of a culture that resents any people who feared God and ordered life by His Word. The Puritans wrote tenderly of marriage, of beauty, of the affections rightly ordered toward God; their practical divinity is a treasury of pastoral wisdom on the inner life. To dismiss them as gloomy tyrants is to slander a people whom Scripture would call, in much, faithful, and to forfeit the riches of their experiential religion.

The opposite corruption idealizes the Puritan colonies as a flawless biblical commonwealth, passing over their real sins: the injustices done to the native peoples and the failure of justice at Salem, where the bounds the law itself sets upon evidence and witness were overrun. The dictionary does neither. It honors the Puritan recovery of covenantal, Word-governed, heart-searching religion (2 Cor 13:5), and it measures the colonies’ failures by the very Scripture they professed, that requires men to do justly and love mercy (Mic 6:8). The children of light are to learn from both.
